approachQuestion.prompt: A row of nonnegative integer strengths must be summarized for every length ℓ from 1 through n. For length ℓ return the largest possible minimum strength among all contiguous intervals of exactly that length. Return n values in increasing length order. Example: [3, 1, 2] returns [3, 1, 1]. Choose the best approach.
constraints: The input is immutable; n is between 1 and 200,000. All integers, indices, counts, and arithmetic results fit in signed 64-bit machine words; comparisons and arithmetic have unit cost.
Input and returned output are excluded from auxiliary space. Working stacks, arrays, and copies count. No hashing is used.

options.text: Find the nearest strictly smaller strength on both sides of every index using ordered stacks. Its full span width w supports its strength; maximize a bucket for width w. Sweep lengths downward, replacing each bucket by the maximum of itself and the next longer bucket.
options.feedback: Each minimum remains feasible at every shorter length within its span. Downward propagation carries that support to lengths not directly represented by a maximal span, and every interval is supported by one of its minimum positions.

options.text: Place each strength in its full-span-width bucket and return the buckets without propagation, filling empty ones with 0.
options.feedback: A widest span also supports shorter lengths. For [2, 2, 2], all strengths have width 3, but lengths 1 and 2 must also return 2.

options.text: For each length ℓ return the minimum of the first ℓ entries.
options.feedback: The best interval need not start at the beginning. For [1, 3], the length-one answer is 3, not 1.

options.text: For each length enumerate all intervals of that length and scan each interval for its minimum.
options.feedback: This is correct but repeatedly inspects overlapping intervals and becomes cubic. Boundary widths allow all lengths to share work.

feedback.reason: Turn maximal validity widths into answers for all shorter lengths through downward propagation.
details: Compute strict-smaller boundaries on both sides, using -1 and n outside the row. Set each width bucket to the largest strength with that maximal width; initialize empty buckets to zero. Sweep from n-1 down to 1 taking the maximum with the next bucket. Return the completed buckets as a separately copied array.

A strength valid for a maximal width is also achievable in every smaller width inside that span. Backward maximum propagation fills widths with no direct candidate. Zero initialization is safe because strengths are nonnegative.

Sweep lengths downward, replacing each bucket by the maximum of itself and the next longer bucket.”: Each minimum remains feasible at every shorter length within its span. Downward propagation carries that support to lengths not directly represented by a maximal span, and every interval is supported by one of its minimum positions.

“For each length ℓ return the minimum of the first ℓ entries.”: The best interval need not start at the beginning. For [1, 3], the length-one answer is 3, not 1.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For width-buckets-and-propagation, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the strength count. Allocate boundary arrays, a stack, and n width buckets; copy the final buckets once into the returned output.
constraints: Stack push, pop, and top take amortized constant time using a growable array; each entry uses a constant number of words. Count the working stack, but exclude input and final output. No recursive call stack or hash table is used.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Boundary construction, width buckets, and backward propagation are all linear passes.
details: Each index obtains boundaries through stack pushes and pops charged once per pass. Bucketing writes one candidate per index, and backward propagation visits each width once, so these phases add to O(n), not O(n²). The separate boundary arrays, width buckets and working stack remain O(n) auxiliary storage after excluding the copied output.
